case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s presented with painful erythematous plaques on her trunk (Figure, A). Skin lesions developed 2 months earlier and progressively spread. She reported abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and vaginal bleeding. A solid mass on her lower abdomen that had been palpable about 10 years prior had rapidly increased in size within the past few months. Physical examination revealed erythematous plaques on the right chest and flank without warmth. Punch biopsy of a lesion from the chest was sent for histopathological examination (Figure, B and C).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous plaques involving the right chest and flank at the initial presentation. B and C, Large atypical cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm forming papillary and glandular architectures are present in the deep dermis; lymphovascular invasion was observed in the superficial and deep dermis (hematoxylin-eosin). D, Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis showing a large heterogeneous mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle (blue arrowhead) and cystic lesion in the left ovary (pink arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Results of histopathological examination showed atypical cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles forming a glandular architecture in the deep dermis, and lymphovascular invasion was observed (Figure, B and C). Immunohistochemical staining results were positive for CK7 and negative for CK20, estrogen receptors (ERs), GATA-binding protein 3, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, Wilms tumor 1 (WT1), and thyroid transcription factor-1. Findings from chest and abdominopelvic computed tomography revealed a 13-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle and a 3-cm ovarian cystic lesion (Figure, D). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography findings revealed intense abnormal18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the abdominal wall, lung, liver, and lymph nodes. Laboratory examinations revealed increased concentrations of lactate dehydrogenase (558 U/L; reference, 135-214 U/L; to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), cancer antigen 15-3 (143.8 U/mL; reference, <26.4 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and cancer antigen 125 (2528 U/mL; reference, <35 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level (2.2 ng/mL; reference, <6 ng/mL; to convert to μg/L, multiply by 1.0). The patient underwent debulking surgery, and pathologic examination revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma positive for MOC31, napsin A, and PAX8, and negative for calretinin, WT1, CK5/6, ERs, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, and p53. The patient was diagnosed with primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma (PPCCC) with multiple distant metastases. She underwent chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin, but the disease progressed continuously. Another metastatic lesion developed in her abdomen. Despite treatment with topotecan and cisplatin, she died 6 months after the initial diagnosis. Primary peritoneal carcinoma (PPC) is a rare malignant epithelial tumor, and PPCCC is an extremely rare subtype of PPC, with only 15 cases, to our knowledge, having been reported since 1990.1Because of its rarity, the clinical characteristics of PPCCC are not well understood. In the previous reports, all patients with PPCCC were female, and the average age was 53.7 years. The initial symptoms included abdominal pain, distension, and an abdominopelvic solid mass. Imaging studies commonly revealed large heterogeneous cystic and solid masses with a mean size of 13 cm. Histologically, PPCCC closely resembles primary peritoneal serous carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma. For diagnosis, extensive immunohistochemical staining is required. Primary peritoneal serous carcinoma expresses CK7, ERs, and WT1, but PPCCC is typically negative for WT1.1Malignant mesothelioma is typically positive for CK5/6, calretinin, and WT1, and negative for MOC31, but PPCCC shows the opposite features.1 Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis usually manifests as indurated erythematous to violaceous plaques symmetrically distributed on the lateral trunk and proximal extremities.2Histologically, interstitial and perivascular histiocytic infiltrates with small foci of collagen degeneration are observed in the reticular dermis.3Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is often associated with rheumatic diseases, hematologic disorders, and internal cancers, but pathogenesis of interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is currently not well understood.3Wolf isotopic response is a rare cutaneous reaction in which a new and unrelated dermatosis occurs at the site of a previously healed dermatosis, most commonly in areas of post–varicella-zoster virus scarring.4Histologically, granulomatous and lichenoid reactions were frequently reported.5Cutaneous endometriosis usually manifests as reddish-brown nodules on the umbilicus or a firm mass on the scar site. Histopathological examination shows the columnar epithelium surrounded by stroma, which consists of capillary vessels, fibroblasts, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.6 To our knowledge, cutaneous metastasis of PPCCC has not yet been reported. Primary peritoneal carcinoma most commonly metastasizes within the peritoneal cavity; metastases to the skin, liver, brain, lung, and breast are rarely reported.7Because PPC behaves similarly to ovarian carcinoma,7,8PPC may also manifest with lesions similar to those associated with ovarian carcinomas, such as inflammatory metastases, cicatricial plaques, or cellulitislike or lymphangitislike lesions,9and similar features can be expected in PPCCC. Patients with PPCCC are commonly treated with debulking surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. Primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma is considered to have a poor prognosis because the majority of patients die of the disease within 6 months or experience recurrence within 3 years.10Because of the poor prognosis, prompt diagnosis and optimal treatment are required.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.caption: A, Erythematous plaques involving the right chest and flank at the initial presentation. B and C, Large atypical cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm forming papillary and glandular architectures are present in the deep dermis; lymphovascular invasion was observed in the superficial and deep dermis (hematoxylin-eosin). D, Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis showing a large heterogeneous mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle (blue arrowhead) and cystic lesion in the left ovary (pink arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Results of histopathological examination showed atypical cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles forming a glandular architecture in the deep dermis, and lymphovascular invasion was observed (Figure, B and C). Immunohistochemical staining results were positive for CK7 and negative for CK20, estrogen receptors (ERs), GATA-binding protein 3, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, Wilms tumor 1 (WT1), and thyroid transcription factor-1. Findings from chest and abdominopelvic computed tomography revealed a 13-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle and a 3-cm ovarian cystic lesion (Figure, D). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography findings revealed intense abnormal18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the abdominal wall, lung, liver, and lymph nodes. Laboratory examinations revealed increased concentrations of lactate dehydrogenase (558 U/L; reference, 135-214 U/L; to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), cancer antigen 15-3 (143.8 U/mL; reference, <26.4 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and cancer antigen 125 (2528 U/mL; reference, <35 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level (2.2 ng/mL; reference, <6 ng/mL; to convert to μg/L, multiply by 1.0). The patient underwent debulking surgery, and pathologic examination revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma positive for MOC31, napsin A, and PAX8, and negative for calretinin, WT1, CK5/6, ERs, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, and p53. The patient was diagnosed with primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma (PPCCC) with multiple distant metastases. She underwent chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin, but the disease progressed continuously. Another metastatic lesion developed in her abdomen. Despite treatment with topotecan and cisplatin, she died 6 months after the initial diagnosis. Primary peritoneal carcinoma (PPC) is a rare malignant epithelial tumor, and PPCCC is an extremely rare subtype of PPC, with only 15 cases, to our knowledge, having been reported since 1990.1Because of its rarity, the clinical characteristics of PPCCC are not well understood. In the previous reports, all patients with PPCCC were female, and the average age was 53.7 years. The initial symptoms included abdominal pain, distension, and an abdominopelvic solid mass. Imaging studies commonly revealed large heterogeneous cystic and solid masses with a mean size of 13 cm. Histologically, PPCCC closely resembles primary peritoneal serous carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma. For diagnosis, extensive immunohistochemical staining is required. Primary peritoneal serous carcinoma expresses CK7, ERs, and WT1, but PPCCC is typically negative for WT1.1Malignant mesothelioma is typically positive for CK5/6, calretinin, and WT1, and negative for MOC31, but PPCCC shows the opposite features.1 Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis usually manifests as indurated erythematous to violaceous plaques symmetrically distributed on the lateral trunk and proximal extremities.2Histologically, interstitial and perivascular histiocytic infiltrates with small foci of collagen degeneration are observed in the reticular dermis.3Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is often associated with rheumatic diseases, hematologic disorders, and internal cancers, but pathogenesis of interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is currently not well understood.3Wolf isotopic response is a rare cutaneous reaction in which a new and unrelated dermatosis occurs at the site of a previously healed dermatosis, most commonly in areas of post–varicella-zoster virus scarring.4Histologically, granulomatous and lichenoid reactions were frequently reported.5Cutaneous endometriosis usually manifests as reddish-brown nodules on the umbilicus or a firm mass on the scar site. Histopathological examination shows the columnar epithelium surrounded by stroma, which consists of capillary vessels, fibroblasts, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.6 To our knowledge, cutaneous metastasis of PPCCC has not yet been reported. Primary peritoneal carcinoma most commonly metastasizes within the peritoneal cavity; metastases to the skin, liver, brain, lung, and breast are rarely reported.7Because PPC behaves similarly to ovarian carcinoma,7,8PPC may also manifest with lesions similar to those associated with ovarian carcinomas, such as inflammatory metastases, cicatricial plaques, or cellulitislike or lymphangitislike lesions,9and similar features can be expected in PPCCC. Patients with PPCCC are commonly treated with debulking surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. Primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma is considered to have a poor prognosis because the majority of patients die of the disease within 6 months or experience recurrence within 3 years.10Because of the poor prognosis, prompt diagnosis and optimal treatment are required.

case_info.caption: A, Erythematous plaques involving the right chest and flank at the initial presentation. B and C, Large atypical cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm forming papillary and glandular architectures are present in the deep dermis; lymphovascular invasion was observed in the superficial and deep dermis (hematoxylin-eosin). D, Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis showing a large heterogeneous mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle (blue arrowhead) and cystic lesion in the left ovary (pink arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Results of histopathological examination showed atypical cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles forming a glandular architecture in the deep dermis, and lymphovascular invasion was observed (Figure, B and C). Immunohistochemical staining results were positive for CK7 and negative for CK20, estrogen receptors (ERs), GATA-binding protein 3, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, Wilms tumor 1 (WT1), and thyroid transcription factor-1. Findings from chest and abdominopelvic computed tomography revealed a 13-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right rectus abdominis muscle and a 3-cm ovarian cystic lesion (Figure, D). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography findings revealed intense abnormal18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the abdominal wall, lung, liver, and lymph nodes. Laboratory examinations revealed increased concentrations of lactate dehydrogenase (558 U/L; reference, 135-214 U/L; to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), cancer antigen 15-3 (143.8 U/mL; reference, <26.4 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and cancer antigen 125 (2528 U/mL; reference, <35 U/mL; to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1.0), and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level (2.2 ng/mL; reference, <6 ng/mL; to convert to μg/L, multiply by 1.0). The patient underwent debulking surgery, and pathologic examination revealed poorly differentiated carcinoma positive for MOC31, napsin A, and PAX8, and negative for calretinin, WT1, CK5/6, ERs, gross cystic disease fluid protein 15, and p53. The patient was diagnosed with primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma (PPCCC) with multiple distant metastases. She underwent chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin, but the disease progressed continuously. Another metastatic lesion developed in her abdomen. Despite treatment with topotecan and cisplatin, she died 6 months after the initial diagnosis. Primary peritoneal carcinoma (PPC) is a rare malignant epithelial tumor, and PPCCC is an extremely rare subtype of PPC, with only 15 cases, to our knowledge, having been reported since 1990.1Because of its rarity, the clinical characteristics of PPCCC are not well understood. In the previous reports, all patients with PPCCC were female, and the average age was 53.7 years. The initial symptoms included abdominal pain, distension, and an abdominopelvic solid mass. Imaging studies commonly revealed large heterogeneous cystic and solid masses with a mean size of 13 cm. Histologically, PPCCC closely resembles primary peritoneal serous carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma. For diagnosis, extensive immunohistochemical staining is required. Primary peritoneal serous carcinoma expresses CK7, ERs, and WT1, but PPCCC is typically negative for WT1.1Malignant mesothelioma is typically positive for CK5/6, calretinin, and WT1, and negative for MOC31, but PPCCC shows the opposite features.1 Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis usually manifests as indurated erythematous to violaceous plaques symmetrically distributed on the lateral trunk and proximal extremities.2Histologically, interstitial and perivascular histiocytic infiltrates with small foci of collagen degeneration are observed in the reticular dermis.3Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is often associated with rheumatic diseases, hematologic disorders, and internal cancers, but pathogenesis of interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is currently not well understood.3Wolf isotopic response is a rare cutaneous reaction in which a new and unrelated dermatosis occurs at the site of a previously healed dermatosis, most commonly in areas of post–varicella-zoster virus scarring.4Histologically, granulomatous and lichenoid reactions were frequently reported.5Cutaneous endometriosis usually manifests as reddish-brown nodules on the umbilicus or a firm mass on the scar site. Histopathological examination shows the columnar epithelium surrounded by stroma, which consists of capillary vessels, fibroblasts, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.6 To our knowledge, cutaneous metastasis of PPCCC has not yet been reported. Primary peritoneal carcinoma most commonly metastasizes within the peritoneal cavity; metastases to the skin, liver, brain, lung, and breast are rarely reported.7Because PPC behaves similarly to ovarian carcinoma,7,8PPC may also manifest with lesions similar to those associated with ovarian carcinomas, such as inflammatory metastases, cicatricial plaques, or cellulitislike or lymphangitislike lesions,9and similar features can be expected in PPCCC. Patients with PPCCC are commonly treated with debulking surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. Primary peritoneal clear cell carcinoma is considered to have a poor prognosis because the majority of patients die of the disease within 6 months or experience recurrence within 3 years.10Because of the poor prognosis, prompt diagnosis and optimal treatment are required.
